## 1. Purpose

This module analyzes the *Coffea arabica* phenotypes used as
responses in the real-data genomic prediction workflow. The experiment contains
three annual evaluations, 13 experimental progenies, two checks, and an
augmented-block structure.

The module has four goals:

- **Describe the experiment:** make the years, progenies, checks, blocks,
  populations, plants, and traits explicit.
- **Document the reference mixed model:** present fixed year means and the five
  random components in the phenotypic mixed model.
- **Present saved variance components and BLUPs:** quantify progeny, permanent plant,
  population, block, progeny-by-year, and residual variation.
- **Prepare the genomic-prediction targets:** retain one BLUP for each of the 195
  target plants and each trait.

The tutorial proceeds in this order: **inspect the experimental records →
describe the traits → specify the mixed model → document its existing estimation
procedure → summarize the fitted effects → assemble the individual BLUPs →
identify the outputs supplied to the genomic audit**. Each section introduces
the objects used in the next step, while genotype matching is reserved for R02.

No marker data are used in this module. Genomic information enters only after
this phenotypic stage has been completed.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

## 2. Software packages

The phenotypic analysis uses three packages:

- **`knitr`** formats experimental summaries and model results as HTML tables.
- **`ggplot2`** displays the distributions of the individual BLUPs.
- **`ggthemes`** applies the same visual style used in the simulated workflow.

The original mixed-model equations, variance-component updates, and stopping
rule are documented below; model fitting is not performed when rendering.

```{r packages, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
```

## 3. Experimental data

The original tab-delimited file contains 684 phenotypic observations and 11
variables. Each of the 228 permanent plant identifiers is recorded in 2014,
2015, and 2016. The following steps inspect these records without changing
their values or their order in the full data set.

### 3.1 Reading and inspecting phenotypic records

The source file is read with its original column names. Rows represent
observations of individual plants in a particular evaluation year; the same
plant therefore appears in more than one row.

```{r read-phenotypes}
# Read the canonical phenotypic observations from the original data file.
PHENOTYPE_INPUT <- "data/dados_reais/coffee_phenotypes.txt"

phenotype <- read.delim(
  PHENOTYPE_INPUT,
  header = TRUE,
  sep = "\t",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

To illustrate the repeated evaluations, the example below displays the first
three distinct plant identifiers in the source file, including one check and
two experimental plants. It selects only a small display sample; subsequent
analyses continue to use the complete `phenotype` data frame.

```{r phenotype-record-sample}
# Follow the first three plant identifiers across the three evaluation years.
phenotype_example <- phenotype[
  phenotype$ID_Planta %in% head(unique(phenotype$ID_Planta), 3L),
  c("ID_Planta", "Ano", "Progenie", "Planta", "Bloco", "Cer", "BM", "LP"),
  drop = FALSE
]

# Order the display by permanent plant identifier and evaluation year.
phenotype_example <- phenotype_example[
  order(phenotype_example$ID_Planta, phenotype_example$Ano),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

rownames(phenotype_example) <- NULL

phenotype_example |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Original phenotypic records for three plants evaluated in 2014–2016"
  )
```

The sample shows that `ID_Planta` stays constant while `Ano` and the observed
phenotypic responses change. It also distinguishes the permanent plant
identifier from the plant number within a progeny.

### 3.2 Variable dictionary

The source contains the following fields. Numerical identifiers are recorded as
integers, but population, block, progeny, and year codes represent categories or
experimental factors rather than continuous measurements.

| Variable | Type and observed coding | Meaning and role |
|---|---|---|
| `Observacao` | Integer; 1–684 | Unique row identifier for each recorded observation. |
| `Progenie` | Integer; 1–15 | Progeny: 1–13 experimental, 14–15 checks; random effect in the model. |
| `Ano` | Integer; 2014, 2015, 2016 | Evaluation year; fixed effect in the model. |
| `ID_Planta` | Integer; 228 distinct IDs | Permanent identifier of the same plant across years; random plant effect. |
| `Populacao` | Integer codes; 1–4 | Population identifier; random effect in the model. |
| `Bloco` | Integer codes; 1–7 | Experimental block identifier; random effect in the model. |
| `Progenie_Ano` | Text; e.g., `14_2016` | Progeny-by-year combination (45 distinct levels); random interaction effect. |
| `Planta` | Integer; 1–15 | Plant number within a progeny; not a unique identifier across the check plants. |
| `Cer` | Integer scores; 1–5 | Cercosporiosis response. |
| `BM` | Integer scores; 1–5 | Leaf-miner incidence response. |
| `LP` | Numeric; 0–21.5 | Production-related response. The seven zeros indicate non-observations; positive observed values range from 0.1 to 21.5. |

Table: Variables and observed coding in the phenotypic data

No empty fields or explicit `NA` entries occur in the original file. The seven
zero-coded `LP` records all occur in 2015; `Cer` and `BM` have no zeros.
The source file does not specify measurement units or detailed scoring
protocols, so those details are not inferred here.

### 3.3 Experimental structure and augmented blocks

The 684 records correspond to 228 permanent plant identifiers evaluated in
2014, 2015, and 2016. Progenies 1-13 form the genomic-prediction population.
Progenies 14 and 15 are checks in the augmented-block experiment and remain in
the phenotypic mixed-model fit.

The pair `ID_Planta` and `Ano` uniquely identifies every observation. By
contrast, some check plants share the same `Progenie` and `Planta` codes;
those fields must not be used on their own to identify individual plants.

```{r target-and-check-progenies}
target <- phenotype[phenotype$Progenie %in% 1:13, , drop = FALSE]
checks <- phenotype[phenotype$Progenie %in% 14:15, , drop = FALSE]
```

The following table describes the experimental design and study population.

```{r experimental-structure}
structure_summary <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Phenotypic observations", "Evaluation years", "Progenies",
    "Experimental progenies", "Check progenies", "Permanent plant identifiers",
    "Target plants", "Check plant identifiers", "Blocks", "Populations",
    "Progeny-by-year levels"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(phenotype), length(unique(phenotype$Ano)),
    length(unique(phenotype$Progenie)), length(unique(target$Progenie)),
    length(unique(checks$Progenie)), length(unique(phenotype$ID_Planta)),
    length(unique(target$ID_Planta)), length(unique(checks$ID_Planta)),
    length(unique(phenotype$Bloco)), length(unique(phenotype$Populacao)),
    length(unique(phenotype$Progenie_Ano))
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

structure_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Experimental structure of the coffee phenotypic data",
    col.names = c(
      "Quantity", "Value"
    )
  )
```

For the experimental progenies,

\[
13\ \text{progenies}\times15\ \text{plants}=195\ \text{target plants}.
\]

`ID_Planta` therefore identifies the same individual plant across all three
evaluation years.

## 4. Phenotypic traits

The three phenotypic responses are `Cer`, `BM`, and `LP`. They are summarized
by trait and evaluation year before model fitting. Because zero denotes an
absent observation, descriptive statistics use only observed values. The `Zero_count` field documents the
zero-coded records separately (seven for `LP`), consistently with the
mixed-model analysis in Section 6.

### 4.1 Overall phenotypic summaries

The overall table displays the number of observed records, mean, dispersion,
and range for each trait. Zero-coded non-observations are counted separately.

```{r trait-summary-overall}
# Identify the phenotypic traits before calculating their summaries.
traits <- c("Cer", "BM", "LP")

trait_summary <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {

  x <- phenotype[[trait]]
  x_observed <- x[is.finite(x) & x != 0]

  trait_summary <- rbind(
    trait_summary,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      N = length(x_observed),
      Mean = mean(x_observed),
      SD = stats::sd(x_observed),
      Minimum = min(x_observed),
      Maximum = max(x_observed),
      Zero_count = sum(x == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

rownames(trait_summary) <- NULL

trait_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Observed phenotypic summaries with separate zero-coded missing counts",
    col.names = c(
      "Trait", "N", "Mean",
      "SD", "Minimum", "Maximum",
      "Zero-coded missing"
    )
  )
```

The first table summarizes each characteristic; the next one preserves the evaluation-year breakdown.

### 4.2 Phenotypic summaries by evaluation year

The annual summaries preserve differences among the 2014, 2015, and 2016
measurements without pooling their distributions.

```{r trait-summary-by-year}
year_summary <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {

  for (year in sort(unique(phenotype$Ano))) {

    x <- phenotype[
      phenotype$Ano == year,
      trait
    ]
    x_observed <- x[is.finite(x) & x != 0]

    year_summary <- rbind(
      year_summary,
      data.frame(
        Trait = trait,
        Year = year,
        N = length(x_observed),
        Zero_count = sum(x == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
        Mean = mean(x_observed),
        SD = stats::sd(x_observed),
        Minimum = min(x_observed),
        Maximum = max(x_observed),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

rownames(year_summary) <- NULL

year_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Observed phenotypic summaries by year with separate missing counts",
    col.names = c(
      "Trait", "Year", "N",
      "Zero-coded missing", "Mean", "SD",
      "Minimum", "Maximum"
    )
  )
```

The first table describes the available observations for each trait; the
second retains the evaluation year so that differences in data availability
are not hidden by an overall summary. The seven zero-coded `LP` records are
reported as missing observations rather than phenotypic measurements. These tables describe the phenotypic input without changing the observations
used by the mixed model.

## 5. Phenotypic mixed model

The model includes fixed evaluation-year means and five random-effect terms.
Its statistical formulation is the same for all three phenotypic traits; the
response observations are prepared separately before estimation.

Each trait is analyzed separately with

\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{u}
+
\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{g}
+
\mathbf{W}\mathbf{p}
+
\mathbf{V}\mathbf{r}
+
\mathbf{T}\mathbf{b}
+
\mathbf{R}\mathbf{i}
+
\mathbf{e},
\]

where:

- \(\mathbf{u}\): fixed evaluation-year means;
- \(\mathbf{g}\): random progeny effects;
- \(\mathbf{p}\): random permanent individual plant effects;
- \(\mathbf{r}\): random population effects;
- \(\mathbf{b}\): random block effects;
- \(\mathbf{i}\): random progeny-by-year interaction effects;
- \(\mathbf{e}\): residual variation.

The model separates permanent differences among plants from annual and
experimental sources of variation.

| Model component | Data field | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed year | `Ano` | Fixed |
| Progeny | `Progenie` | Random |
| Permanent individual plant | `ID_Planta` | Random |
| Population | `Populacao` | Random |
| Block | `Bloco` | Random |
| Progeny x year | `Progenie_Ano` | Random |
| Residual | Not applicable | Residual |

Table: Terms in the phenotypic mixed model

`Planta` is retained for identification but is not fitted as an additional
random effect because `ID_Planta` already represents the permanent individual
plant.

## 6. Trait-specific data preparation

The response data must be prepared before constructing the mixed-model
equations. In the field-data coding used here, zero denotes an absent
observation. The fitted models therefore use all 684 `Cer` and `BM` records
and exclude the seven zero-coded `LP` records, retaining 677 observations
for `LP`.

The following chunk creates one data set per trait, places the corresponding
phenotypic response in `y`, and retains only its observed values. The list
`analysis_data` then supplies those three data sets to the fitting loop.

```{r prepare-traits}
cer_data <- phenotype
cer_data$y <- as.numeric(cer_data$Cer)
cer_data <- cer_data[
  is.finite(cer_data$y) & cer_data$y != 0,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

bm_data <- phenotype
bm_data$y <- as.numeric(bm_data$BM)
bm_data <- bm_data[
  is.finite(bm_data$y) & bm_data$y != 0,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

lp_data <- phenotype
lp_data$y <- as.numeric(lp_data$LP)
lp_data <- lp_data[
  is.finite(lp_data$y) & lp_data$y != 0,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

analysis_data <- list(
  Cer = cer_data,
  BM = bm_data,
  LP = lp_data
)
```

The table below reports the observations entering the previously fitted trait models.

```{r records-used-table}
records_used <- data.frame(
  Trait = c("Cer", "BM", "LP"),
  Records_available = rep(nrow(phenotype), 3),
  Records_used = c(
    nrow(cer_data),
    nrow(bm_data),
    nrow(lp_data)
  ),
  Records_excluded = c(
    nrow(phenotype) - nrow(cer_data),
    nrow(phenotype) - nrow(bm_data),
    nrow(phenotype) - nrow(lp_data)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

records_used |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "Records entering each trait-specific mixed model",
    col.names = c(
      "Trait", "Available", "Used",
      "Excluded"
    )
  )
```

The table above documents the numbers of records available, retained, and
excluded for each phenotypic response. The full source data remain unchanged;
only the trait-specific inputs to the original fitted models differ.

## 7. REML variance-component estimation

The fitting procedure starts from variance proportions of 0.10 for each random
effect and 0.50 for the residual. Thus the initial variance ratio for every
random component is

\[
\lambda_j=\frac{0.50}{0.10}=5.
\]

At each iteration, the mixed-model equations are solved and the residual
variance is updated by

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_e^2
=
\frac{
\mathbf{e}'\mathbf{e}
+
\sum_j \lambda_j\mathbf{u}_j'\mathbf{u}_j
}{
n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X})
},
\]

while each random-effect variance is updated by

\[
\widehat{\sigma}_j^2
=
\frac{
\mathbf{u}_j'\mathbf{u}_j
+
\widehat{\sigma}_e^2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{C}_{jj})
}{q_j}.
\]

The loop stops when the largest absolute change among the five random variance
proportions is smaller than or equal to the trait-specific tolerance.

### 7.1 Trait-specific fitting controls

The numerical tolerances belong to the mixed-model fitting procedure, not to
the definition of the phenotypic variables. For `Cer` and `BM`, the existing
tolerance is 0.05; for `LP`, it is 0.0001. The original fitting procedure
uses at most 500 iterations and starts from five random-effect proportions of
0.10 and a residual proportion of 0.50. These settings are documented next to
the algorithm in which they are used.

```{r model-fitting-tolerances}
tolerance <- c(
  Cer = 0.05,
  BM = 0.05,
  LP = 0.0001
)
```

The table below summarizes the stored fitting controls for each trait.

| Trait | Tolerance | Zero-coded missing |
|---|---:|---|
| `Cer` | 0.05 | TRUE |
| `BM` | 0.05 | TRUE |
| `LP` | 0.0001 | TRUE |

Table: Trait-specific fitting settings

### 7.2 Mixed-model fitting procedure

The original algorithm proceeds through five stages within a single fitting
loop, repeated separately for `Cer`, `BM`, and `LP`:

1. **Incidence matrices:** identify factor levels in each trait's prepared
   data, build `X` and the five random-effect incidence matrices with
   `model.matrix()`, combine them in `W`, and record the coefficient indices
   for each random effect.
2. **Initialization:** assign 0.10 to each of the five random-effect variance
   proportions and 0.50 to the residual, then initialize the iteration history.
3. **Mixed-model iteration:** calculate the current variance ratios
   `lambda_*`, assemble the penalty matrix, solve the mixed-model equations,
   obtain fitted values and residuals, and estimate residual and random-effect
   variances.
4. **Update and convergence:** combine the six estimated variances, normalize
   them into `new_props`, calculate the stored deviance, and compare the
   largest absolute change among the **five random-effect proportions** with
   `tolerance[[trait]]`. The procedure stops on convergence or reports failure
   if the tolerance is not reached within 500 iterations.
5. **Fitted solutions:** label the fixed-year and random-effect coefficients
   by their observed levels, then retain the estimates, residuals, diagnostics,
   iteration history, and tolerance in `fits[[trait]]`.

The mathematical quantities introduced above have direct counterparts in the
code. The `lambda_*` values are the residual-to-random variance ratios, while
`M <- crossprod(W) + penalty` is the penalized mixed-model system and
`C <- solve(M)` is its inverse. The residual variance equation is implemented
through `penalized_ss / df_reml`; the five random-effect variance updates use
the estimated effects and the corresponding diagonal blocks of `C`. Here,
`df_reml` equals the number of retained observations minus `ncol(X)`. Since
the three evaluation-year columns in `X` are linearly independent, this
matches the `n - rank(X)` denominator shown above.

The original fitting procedure is preserved as one continuous algorithm to
make the dependencies among its stages explicit. It remains `eval=FALSE`:
the tables in the next sections come from the previously saved RDS files,
not from a new model fit during site rendering.

```{r fit-models, eval=FALSE}
fits <- list()

for (trait in traits) {

  d <- analysis_data[[trait]]

# Stage 1: incidence matrices and effect indices.
  year_levels <- unique(d$Ano)
  progeny_levels <- unique(d$Progenie)
  plant_levels <- unique(d$ID_Planta)
  population_levels <- unique(d$Populacao)
  block_levels <- unique(d$Bloco)
  progeny_year_levels <- unique(d$Progenie_Ano)

  X <- model.matrix(
    ~ 0 + factor(Ano, levels = year_levels),
    data = d
  )

  Z_progeny <- model.matrix(
    ~ 0 + factor(Progenie, levels = progeny_levels),
    data = d
  )

  Z_plant <- model.matrix(
    ~ 0 + factor(ID_Planta, levels = plant_levels),
    data = d
  )

  Z_population <- model.matrix(
    ~ 0 + factor(Populacao, levels = population_levels),
    data = d
  )

  Z_block <- model.matrix(
    ~ 0 + factor(Bloco, levels = block_levels),
    data = d
  )

  Z_progeny_year <- model.matrix(
    ~ 0 + factor(Progenie_Ano, levels = progeny_year_levels),
    data = d
  )

  # Combine the fixed and random design matrices in coefficient order.
  W <- cbind(
    X,
    Z_progeny,
    Z_plant,
    Z_population,
    Z_block,
    Z_progeny_year
  )

  # Locate each random-effect block within the joint matrix W.
  p <- ncol(X)

  start_progeny <- p + 1L
  end_progeny <- start_progeny + ncol(Z_progeny) - 1L

  start_plant <- end_progeny + 1L
  end_plant <- start_plant + ncol(Z_plant) - 1L

  start_population <- end_plant + 1L
  end_population <- start_population + ncol(Z_population) - 1L

  start_block <- end_population + 1L
  end_block <- start_block + ncol(Z_block) - 1L

  start_progeny_year <- end_block + 1L
  end_progeny_year <- start_progeny_year + ncol(Z_progeny_year) - 1L

  idx_progeny <- start_progeny:end_progeny
  idx_plant <- start_plant:end_plant
  idx_population <- start_population:end_population
  idx_block <- start_block:end_block
  idx_progeny_year <- start_progeny_year:end_progeny_year

# Stage 2: initialize variance proportions and the iteration history.
  old_props <- c(
    Progenie = 0.10,
    ID_Planta = 0.10,
    Populacao = 0.10,
    Bloco = 0.10,
    Progenie_Ano = 0.10,
    Residual = 0.50
  )

  history <- data.frame(
    Trait = character(),
    Iteration = integer(),
    Maximum_change = numeric(),
    Tolerance = numeric(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

# Stage 3: iteratively solve equations and estimate variance components.
  for (iteration in seq_len(500L)) {

    # Form the current residual-to-random variance ratios.
    lambda_progeny <- old_props["Residual"] / old_props["Progenie"]
    lambda_plant <- old_props["Residual"] / old_props["ID_Planta"]
    lambda_population <- old_props["Residual"] / old_props["Populacao"]
    lambda_block <- old_props["Residual"] / old_props["Bloco"]
    lambda_progeny_year <- old_props["Residual"] / old_props["Progenie_Ano"]

    penalty <- matrix(
      0,
      nrow = ncol(W),
      ncol = ncol(W)
    )

    penalty[idx_progeny, idx_progeny] <- diag(
      as.numeric(lambda_progeny),
      length(idx_progeny)
    )

    penalty[idx_plant, idx_plant] <- diag(
      as.numeric(lambda_plant),
      length(idx_plant)
    )

    penalty[idx_population, idx_population] <- diag(
      as.numeric(lambda_population),
      length(idx_population)
    )

    penalty[idx_block, idx_block] <- diag(
      as.numeric(lambda_block),
      length(idx_block)
    )

    penalty[idx_progeny_year, idx_progeny_year] <- diag(
      as.numeric(lambda_progeny_year),
      length(idx_progeny_year)
    )

    # Solve the penalized mixed-model equations and recover the residuals.
    M <- crossprod(W) + penalty
    rhs <- crossprod(W, d$y)

    coefficients <- solve(M, rhs)
    C <- solve(M)

    fitted_values <- as.numeric(W %*% coefficients)
    residuals <- d$y - fitted_values

    u_progeny <- coefficients[idx_progeny]
    u_plant <- coefficients[idx_plant]
    u_population <- coefficients[idx_population]
    u_block <- coefficients[idx_block]
    u_progeny_year <- coefficients[idx_progeny_year]

    # Update the residual variance using the penalized sum of squares.
    penalized_ss <- (
      sum(residuals^2) +
      as.numeric(lambda_progeny) * sum(u_progeny^2) +
      as.numeric(lambda_plant) * sum(u_plant^2) +
      as.numeric(lambda_population) * sum(u_population^2) +
      as.numeric(lambda_block) * sum(u_block^2) +
      as.numeric(lambda_progeny_year) * sum(u_progeny_year^2)
    )

    df_reml <- nrow(d) - ncol(X)
    residual_variance <- penalized_ss / df_reml

    # Update each random variance with its effects and C diagonal block.
    V_progeny <- (
      sum(u_progeny^2) +
      residual_variance *
        sum(diag(C[idx_progeny, idx_progeny, drop = FALSE]))
    ) / length(idx_progeny)

    V_plant <- (
      sum(u_plant^2) +
      residual_variance *
        sum(diag(C[idx_plant, idx_plant, drop = FALSE]))
    ) / length(idx_plant)

    V_population <- (
      sum(u_population^2) +
      residual_variance *
        sum(diag(C[idx_population, idx_population, drop = FALSE]))
    ) / length(idx_population)

    V_block <- (
      sum(u_block^2) +
      residual_variance *
        sum(diag(C[idx_block, idx_block, drop = FALSE]))
    ) / length(idx_block)

    V_progeny_year <- (
      sum(u_progeny_year^2) +
      residual_variance *
        sum(diag(C[
          idx_progeny_year,
          idx_progeny_year,
          drop = FALSE
        ]))
    ) / length(idx_progeny_year)

# Stage 4: normalize variances, evaluate convergence, and record history.
    components <- c(
      Progenie = V_progeny,
      ID_Planta = V_plant,
      Populacao = V_population,
      Bloco = V_block,
      Progenie_Ano = V_progeny_year,
      Residual = residual_variance
    )

    phenotypic_variance <- sum(components)
    new_props <- components / phenotypic_variance

    lambda_new <- residual_variance / components[
      c(
        "Progenie",
        "ID_Planta",
        "Populacao",
        "Bloco",
        "Progenie_Ano"
      )
    ]

    logdet_M <- as.numeric(
      determinant(
        M,
        logarithm = TRUE
      )$modulus
    )

    deviance <- (
      df_reml * (1 + log(residual_variance)) +
      logdet_M -
      (
        length(idx_progeny) * log(lambda_new["Progenie"]) +
        length(idx_plant) * log(lambda_new["ID_Planta"]) +
        length(idx_population) * log(lambda_new["Populacao"]) +
        length(idx_block) * log(lambda_new["Bloco"]) +
        length(idx_progeny_year) * log(lambda_new["Progenie_Ano"])
      )
    )

    # Only the five random-effect proportions enter the stopping criterion.
    random_change <- max(
      abs(
        new_props[
          c(
            "Progenie",
            "ID_Planta",
            "Populacao",
            "Bloco",
            "Progenie_Ano"
          )
        ] -
        old_props[
          c(
            "Progenie",
            "ID_Planta",
            "Populacao",
            "Bloco",
            "Progenie_Ano"
          )
        ]
      )
    )

    history <- rbind(
      history,
      data.frame(
        Trait = trait,
        Iteration = iteration,
        Maximum_change = random_change,
        Tolerance = tolerance[[trait]],
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )

    if (random_change <= tolerance[[trait]]) {
      break
    }

    old_props <- new_props
  }

  if (random_change > tolerance[[trait]]) {
    stop(
      trait,
      ": stopping rule not reached within 500 iterations."
    )
  }

  beta <- coefficients[seq_len(p)]
  names(beta) <- as.character(year_levels)

  names(u_progeny) <- as.character(progeny_levels)
  names(u_plant) <- as.character(plant_levels)
  names(u_population) <- as.character(population_levels)
  names(u_block) <- as.character(block_levels)
  names(u_progeny_year) <- as.character(progeny_year_levels)

# Stage 5: retain fitted effects, variance estimates, and iteration history.
  fits[[trait]] <- list(
    trait = trait,
    data = d,
    final = list(
      components = components,
      proportions = new_props,
      beta = beta,
      u = list(
        Progenie = u_progeny,
        ID_Planta = u_plant,
        Populacao = u_population,
        Bloco = u_block,
        Progenie_Ano = u_progeny_year
      ),
      residual = residuals,
      fitted = fitted_values,
      C = C,
      deviance = as.numeric(deviance),
      random_change = random_change
    ),
    history = history,
    iterations = iteration,
    tolerance = tolerance[[trait]]
  )
}
```

The code above documents the original pathway from incidence matrices to
variance updates and fitted effects. It is not executed during site generation.
The following chunk reads the existing RDS outputs used in Sections 8–10;
none of those values are re-estimated in this tutorial build.

```{r load-saved-phenotypic-results}
# Reuse the existing phenotypic results without recalculating the models.
OUTPUT_DIR <- "output/real/phenotype"

variance_components <- readRDS(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_variance_components.rds"))
model_effects <- readRDS(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_model_effects.rds"))
blups <- readRDS(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_blups.rds"))
```

## 8. Variance components and derived ratios

For each trait,

\[
V_f=V_g+V_p+V_r+V_b+V_i+V_e.
\]

The following quantities describe the fitted variance components. The
between-progeny and between-population proportions are calculated separately:

\[
p_{\mathrm{progeny}}=\frac{V_g}{V_f},\qquad
p_{\mathrm{population}}=\frac{V_r}{V_f}.
\]

The persisted fields `h2_progeny`, `h2_population`, and `h2_total` retain
their existing names and numerical values for downstream compatibility. Their
scientific interpretation in this model is as proportions of fitted phenotypic
variance. Specifically, `h2_total` equals \((V_g+V_r)/V_f\), the **combined
progeny-and-population variance proportion**. The model parameterizes these
between-group components separately from the permanent-plant and other effects,
without defining a distinct additive genetic variance component.

The permanent-plant, block, and progeny-by-year proportions correspond to
\(V_p/V_f\), \(V_b/V_f\), and \(V_i/V_f\), respectively. The reported
**Repeatability** is the model-implied correlation between evaluations of
the same plant in distinct years, sharing progeny, plant, population, and
block effects after accounting for fixed year effects:

\[
R_{\mathrm{plant}}=\frac{V_g+V_p+V_r+V_b}{V_f}.
\]

This coefficient therefore quantifies repeated phenotypic agreement under
the fitted experimental structure. The between-group genetic variance
proportions and within-plant repeatability are distinct measures. This
interpretation follows the variance-component model used for *Coffea
arabica* by [Sousa et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2018.01934)
and the distinction between genetic and phenotypic variance in plant-breeding
models discussed by [Piepho and Möhring (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.107.074229).

```{r variance-components, eval=FALSE}
variance_components <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {

  fit <- fits[[trait]]
  components <- fit$final$components
  props <- fit$final$proportions
  Vf <- sum(components)

  variance_components <- rbind(
    variance_components,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      N = nrow(fit$data),
      Iterations = fit$iterations,
      Tolerance = fit$tolerance,
      Deviance = fit$final$deviance,
      V_progeny = components["Progenie"],
      V_plant = components["ID_Planta"],
      V_population = components["Populacao"],
      V_block = components["Bloco"],
      V_progeny_year = components["Progenie_Ano"],
      V_residual = components["Residual"],
      V_phenotypic = Vf,
      h2_progeny = props["Progenie"],
      c2_plant = props["ID_Planta"],
      h2_population = props["Populacao"],
      c2_block = props["Bloco"],
      c2_progeny_year = props["Progenie_Ano"],
      Repeatability = (
        components["Progenie"] +
        components["ID_Planta"] +
        components["Populacao"] +
        components["Bloco"]
      ) / Vf,
      h2_total = (
        components["Progenie"] +
        components["Populacao"]
      ) / Vf,
      Overall_mean = mean(fit$final$beta),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

rownames(variance_components) <- NULL
```

The tables below display saved variance components and derived ratios rather
than re-estimating them.

```{r saved-variance-components}
variance_table <- variance_components[, c("Trait", "N", "Iterations",
  "V_progeny", "V_plant", "V_population", "V_block",
  "V_progeny_year", "V_residual", "V_phenotypic"), drop = FALSE]
variance_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 6,
    caption = "Variance components from the phenotypic mixed model",
    col.names = c("Trait", "N", "Iterations", "Progeny variance",
      "Plant variance", "Population variance", "Block variance",
      "Progeny-by-year variance", "Residual variance",
      "Phenotypic variance")
  )
```

The second table reports model-implied proportions and repeatability from the saved variance components.

```{r saved-variance-ratios}
parameter_table <- variance_components[, c("Trait", "h2_progeny",
  "c2_plant", "h2_population", "c2_block", "c2_progeny_year",
  "Repeatability", "h2_total", "Overall_mean"), drop = FALSE]
parameter_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 6,
    caption = "Model-implied variance proportions and within-plant repeatability",
    col.names = c("Trait", "Progeny proportion", "Plant proportion",
      "Population proportion", "Block proportion",
      "Progeny-by-year proportion", "Plant repeatability",
      "Progeny + population proportion", "Adjusted mean")
  )
```

Separating the variance components from the derived parameters keeps both
tables readable at the width of the tutorial page.

## 9. Fixed year effects

The fixed solutions estimate the adjusted mean for each evaluation year after
the random experimental and biological effects have been accounted for.

The adjusted year means are retrieved from the previously saved model effects.

```{r saved-fixed-year-effects}
fixed_year_effects <- data.frame()
for (trait in traits) {
  beta_year <- model_effects[[trait]]$fixed_year
  fixed_year_effects <- rbind(fixed_year_effects, data.frame(
    Trait = trait, Year = as.integer(names(beta_year)),
    Adjusted_mean = as.numeric(beta_year), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}
fixed_year_effects[
  order(match(fixed_year_effects$Trait, traits), fixed_year_effects$Year),
  , drop = FALSE
] |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
digits = 4,
    caption = "Adjusted fixed means by evaluation year",
    col.names = c("Trait", "Year", "Adjusted mean"))
```

The table above contains one adjusted fixed-year mean for each trait-year
combination. These are solutions for the fixed evaluation-year effects; they
are not the plant-level BLUPs used as genomic-prediction targets. Section 10
combines the relevant fitted components for each target plant into one value
per characteristic.

## 10. BLUPs for the 195 target plants

### 10.1 Individual identity

For progenies 1-13, `ID_Planta` is in one-to-one correspondence with progeny
and plant number and is repeated over the three years.

```{r target-identity}
target_map <- unique(
  target[, c("ID_Planta", "Progenie", "Planta", "Populacao")]
)

target_map <- target_map[
  order(target_map$Progenie, target_map$Planta),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
rownames(target_map) <- NULL

target_map$Phenotype_ID <- sprintf(
  "PROG%02d_PL%02d",
  target_map$Progenie,
  target_map$Planta
)

head(target_map, 15) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    caption = "First 15 target plants used for genomic prediction",
    col.names = c(
      "Plant ID", "Progeny", "Plant",
      "Population", "Phenotype ID"
    )
  )
```

### 10.2 One BLUP per plant

For genomic prediction, one BLUP is retained for each target plant and trait.
The year, block, and progeny-by-year terms describe evaluation-specific or
experimental variation and are not carried forward as permanent plant values.

For plant \(k\), the BLUP is calculated as

\[
\widehat{y}_k =
\widehat{\mu}
+
\widehat{g}_{j(k)}
+
\widehat{p}_k
+
\widehat{r}_{m(k)},
\]

where \(\widehat{\mu}\) is the overall adjusted mean,
\(\widehat{g}_{j(k)}\) is the progeny effect,
\(\widehat{p}_k\) is the permanent individual-plant effect, and
\(\widehat{r}_{m(k)}\) is the population effect.

The code keeps these components explicit so the construction of each BLUP can
be followed directly.

```{r individual-blups, eval=FALSE}
blup_tables <- list()

for (trait in traits) {

  fit <- fits[[trait]]
  u <- fit$final$u
  overall_mean <- mean(fit$final$beta)

  out <- target_map

  out$Progeny_effect <- as.numeric(
    u$Progenie[
      as.character(out$Progenie)
    ]
  )

  out$Plant_effect <- as.numeric(
    u$ID_Planta[
      as.character(out$ID_Planta)
    ]
  )

  out$Population_effect <- as.numeric(
    u$Populacao[
      as.character(out$Populacao)
    ]
  )

  out$BLUP <- (
    overall_mean +
    out$Progeny_effect +
    out$Plant_effect +
    out$Population_effect
  )

  blup_tables[[trait]] <- out
}
```

For `Cer`, the first plants can be inspected together with the three fitted
components that form their BLUP.

```{r blup-components-example}
# Inspect previously saved effects alongside their corresponding stored BLUPs.
cer_components <- head(blups, 15)
cer_components$Progeny_effect <- as.numeric(
  model_effects$Cer$random$Progenie[as.character(cer_components$Progenie)]
)
cer_components$Plant_effect <- as.numeric(
  model_effects$Cer$random$ID_Planta[as.character(cer_components$ID_Planta)]
)
cer_components$Population_effect <- as.numeric(
  model_effects$Cer$random$Populacao[as.character(cer_components$Populacao)]
)
cer_components[, c("Phenotype_ID", "Progenie", "Planta",
  "Progeny_effect", "Plant_effect", "Population_effect", "Cer"),
  drop = FALSE] |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Components of the first 15 Cer BLUPs",
    col.names = c("Phenotype ID", "Progeny", "Plant",
      "Progeny effect", "Plant effect", "Population effect", "BLUP")
  )
```

The three trait-specific BLUP vectors are then placed in a single table with
one row for each of the 195 target plants.

```{r combine-individual-blups, eval=FALSE}
blups <- target_map[
  ,
  c(
    "Phenotype_ID",
    "ID_Planta",
    "Progenie",
    "Planta",
    "Populacao"
  )
]

blups$Cer <- blup_tables$Cer$BLUP
blups$BM <- blup_tables$BM$BLUP
blups$LP <- blup_tables$LP$BLUP

blups <- blups[
  order(
    blups$Progenie,
    blups$Planta
  ),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

rownames(blups) <- NULL
```

The previously obtained individual BLUPs are read from the RDS file and
shown below without recomputing their values.

```{r saved-individual-blups}
head(blups, 15) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" width="100%"',
    digits = 4,
    caption = "First 15 BLUPs prepared for genomic prediction",
    col.names = c("Phenotype ID", "Plant ID", "Progeny",
      "Plant", "Population", "Cer", "BM", "LP")
  )
```

### 10.3 BLUP distributions

The 195 plant-level BLUPs are displayed as trait-specific density curves.
Each facet uses its own numerical scale and summarizes the adjusted phenotypic
targets entering the genomic-prediction workflow.

```{r blup-distributions, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Density distributions of the BLUPs for the 195 target coffee plants.", fig.alt="Three density plots of individual BLUPs for Cer, BM, and LP, displayed in separate panels with trait-specific scales."}
blup_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(Trait = "Cer", BLUP = blups$Cer),
  data.frame(Trait = "BM", BLUP = blups$BM),
  data.frame(Trait = "LP", BLUP = blups$LP)
)
blup_long$Trait <- factor(blup_long$Trait, levels = traits)

p_blup_distribution <- ggplot(
  blup_long,
  aes(
    x = BLUP,
    fill = Trait,
    colour = Trait
  )
) +
  geom_density(
    alpha = 0.28,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gdocs(limits = c("BM", "Cer", "LP")) +
  scale_color_gdocs(limits = c("BM", "Cer", "LP")) +
  labs(
    x = "BLUP",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_gdocs()

print(p_blup_distribution)
```

```{r save-blup-distributions, include=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
FIGURE_DIR <- file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "figures")

ggsave(
  file.path(
    FIGURE_DIR,
    "blup_distributions.tiff"
  ),
  plot = p_blup_distribution,
  device = "tiff",
  width = 9,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

These 195 rows are the phenotypic targets passed to the next real-data module.
Marker information has not been used to estimate or select any of these values.

## 11. Phenotypic results

The phenotypic analysis produced individual BLUPs, variance components,
model effects, descriptive summaries, and run metadata. This tutorial reads
the stored scientific outputs without regenerating them.

The analysis produces the following files under `output/real/phenotype/`.
Each output has a specific role in inspection or in subsequent genomic analyses:

| Output file | Contents and intended use |
|---|---|
| `real_phenotype_blups.rds` | The 195 individual BLUPs for `Cer`, `BM`, and `LP`; direct input to R02. |
| `real_phenotype_blups.csv` | Tabular version of the individual BLUPs for inspection. |
| `real_phenotype_variance_components.rds` | Fitted variance components and derived quantities retained in R format. |
| `real_phenotype_variance_components.csv` | Tabular presentation of those quantities. |
| `real_phenotype_model_effects.rds` | Stored fixed-year solutions and random effects for each trait. |
| `real_phenotype_summary.csv` | Descriptive summaries of the original phenotypic observations. |
| `real_phenotype_run_metadata.rds` | Recorded information about the analysis execution and settings. |
| `figures/blup_distributions.tiff` | High-resolution version of the BLUP distribution figure from Section 10.3. |

Table: Saved phenotypic outputs and their role in the genomic workflow

The individual-BLUP RDS is the phenotypic input consumed by R02. The other
files preserve the fitted effects, descriptive summaries, and execution
metadata. The disabled code blocks document how the original scientific results were saved.

The original analysis exported the individual BLUPs in both formats.

```{r save-individual-blups, eval=FALSE}
utils::write.csv(
  blups,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_blups.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

saveRDS(
  blups,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_blups.rds")
)
```

The estimated variance components were archived as CSV and RDS.

```{r save-variance-components, eval=FALSE}
utils::write.csv(
  variance_components,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_variance_components.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

saveRDS(
  variance_components,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_variance_components.rds")
)
```

The fixed and random effect solutions were stored separately.

```{r save-model-effects, eval=FALSE}
model_effects <- list()

for (trait in traits) {
  model_effects[[trait]] <- list(
    fixed_year = fits[[trait]]$final$beta,
    random = fits[[trait]]$final$u
  )
}

saveRDS(
  model_effects,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_model_effects.rds")
)
```

The phenotypic descriptive statistics were archived.

```{r save-descriptive-summary, eval=FALSE}
utils::write.csv(
  trait_summary,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_summary.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The run metadata identifies the original inputs and fitted settings.

```{r save-run-metadata, eval=FALSE}
run_metadata <- list(
  generated_at = Sys.time(),
  R_version = R.version.string,
  input = PHENOTYPE_INPUT,
  observations = nrow(phenotype),
  years = sort(unique(phenotype$Ano)),
  progenies = sort(unique(phenotype$Progenie)),
  checks = c(14L, 15L),
  target_plants = nrow(blups),
  traits = traits,
  tolerances = tolerance,
  model = paste(
    "fixed Ano; random Progenie + ID_Planta +",
    "Populacao + Bloco + Progenie_Ano"
  )
)

saveRDS(
  run_metadata,
  file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "real_phenotype_run_metadata.rds")
)
```

The central product is `real_phenotype_blups.rds`, containing exactly 195 target
plants and the three trait BLUPs. Genotype matching and marker quality control
are performed only in the next stage.

## 12. Summary of the phenotypic analysis

The phenotypic analysis comprises:

- the canonical input contains 684 observations from 2014-2016;
- the two checks remain in the mixed-model fit;
- year is fixed;
- progeny, permanent individual plant, population, block, and progeny-by-year
  interaction are random;
- zero-coded non-observations are excluded from mixed-model fitting (seven `LP` records);
- 195 target plants receive one BLUP for each trait;
- no genomic information is used before phenotypic adjustment is complete.

The resulting BLUP table is the phenotypic input to the real-data genomic
workflow.

In **R02 (`real_data_audit.Rmd`)**, the 195 individual BLUP records are matched
to the Capture-Seq genotype profiles using progeny and plant identifiers.
That module applies the specified SNP quality-control rules and prepares a
common genotype-and-BLUP object for cross-validation and the GBLUP and ANN
methods. Phenotypic mixed-model fitting is performed only in R01.
